stem: A team must extract invoice fields, validate them against a schema, then write to a database. The steps are identical for every invoice. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A prompt-chaining workflow with fixed steps in code
An autonomous agent that decides its own steps each run
A manager agent delegating to three specialist subagents
An evaluator-optimizer loop that refines until validation passes

explanation: The steps are known in advance and identical every run, which is the definition of a workflow. Agent and hierarchy options add cost, latency, and variability for nothing. Evaluator-optimizer applies where iteration improves quality, not where the path is fixed.
author: legacy

stem: A research agent runs searches returning 40,000 tokens of raw results. After several searches its answers degrade. What is the primary architectural reason to move searching into a subagent?

options.text: Subagents run faster because they execute in parallel
Each subagent has its own context window, so raw results never enter the parent's context
Subagents can use models the parent cannot access
Subagents bypass rate limits with a separate connection pool

explanation: Context isolation is the primary reason; the parent receives only the distilled summary. Parallelism is a secondary benefit, and the other two describe capabilities subagents don't have.
author: legacy

stem: A support-ticket pipeline classifies each incoming ticket into billing, technical, or account-access, then hands it to a category-specific prompt tuned for that ticket type. Every ticket follows this same two-step flow, though the specialized prompt used in step two differs meaningfully depending on the category. Which architecture fits this pipeline?

options.text: A single fixed prompt chain that runs the same two prompts on every ticket regardless of category
Routing: classify the ticket, then dispatch it to the prompt built for that category
An autonomous agent that decides at runtime how many classification passes to run
An orchestrator-workers design where a central call invents ticket categories on the fly

explanation: Routing fits because the categories are fixed but genuinely need different downstream handling -- that's the definition of routing, not plain chaining. Option A ignores the stated per-category difference in step two, collapsing routing into a single fixed chain. Option C adds agent-level runtime flexibility a fixed two-step flow never needs. Option D misapplies orchestrator-workers, which decides subtasks at runtime -- here the three categories are already known in advance.
author: v1-new

stem: An engineering-metrics agent must read a 200,000-line CI log to isolate the root cause of a flaky test, then hand a two-paragraph summary back to the parent conversation. The team wants to guarantee the parent's context never fills up with raw log lines, no matter how long the log-scanning takes. Which choice best satisfies that guarantee?

options.text: Increase the parent's context window so it can hold the entire log alongside the rest of the conversation
Enable prompt caching on the log content so repeated reads are cheaper
Run the log-scanning in a subagent with its own context window and return only the distilled summary
Run the log-scanning in a subagent so it can execute in parallel with the rest of the pipeline

explanation: A subagent with its own window keeps the raw log isolated; only the condensed summary re-enters the parent's context, which is the guarantee the team wants. A bigger window still fills up with raw lines eventually and doesn't prevent pollution. Prompt caching is a cost/latency optimization -- cached content still occupies context, it doesn't isolate it. Framing the subagent's value as parallel execution names the secondary benefit, not the primary reason, and there's nothing else described running concurrently for it to parallelize against.
author: v1-new

stem: A team is weighing whether to add a manager agent that delegates a task to three specialist subagents, when a single call already handles that task adequately today. Select the two costs this hierarchy specifically introduces that the single-call design does not have.

options.text: Additional token cost and latency at every manager-to-worker hop
Errors a worker makes can propagate upward and compound through the manager's synthesis step
The system permanently loses the ability to call external tools
The model's underlying context-window limit becomes smaller than before

explanation: Hop cost/latency and compounding worker error are the two costs a manager/subagent hierarchy actually adds over a single call. Losing tool-calling ability is false -- hierarchy depth doesn't affect tool access. A shrinking context-window limit is also false -- that's a fixed model property, untouched by how many subagents sit underneath a manager. Both wrong options borrow real-sounding constraints from elsewhere that don't actually apply here.
author: v1-new

stem: A code-review pipeline must run three checks in the exact same order on every single pull request with no exceptions: lint, then type-check, then test. Which implementation actually guarantees that ordering holds every time?

options.text: A system prompt instructing an agent to always run lint, type-check, then test in that order
An evaluator-optimizer loop that keeps retrying the three checks until all of them pass
A manager agent that decides at runtime which of the three checks are relevant to run
Fixed code that calls lint, then type-check, then test, with no model in the decision path

explanation: Only code with no model in the decision path guarantees the order, which is what 'must ... with no exceptions' demands. A system-prompt instruction is a request the model can fail to follow, not a guarantee. An evaluator-optimizer loop assumes criteria to iteratively refine against, which doesn't apply to a fixed three-step checklist, and retries don't guarantee ordering either. A manager deciding which checks are relevant introduces exactly the runtime variability the requirement rules out.
author: v1-new

stem: A document-tagging task applies the exact same three tags via the same three tools to every document, with no variation across runs. A colleague argues for building this as an autonomous agent instead of a fixed workflow because, in their words, agents are 'more flexible and more modern.' What is the strongest architectural counterargument?

options.text: Flexibility has no payoff when the steps and tools are already fully known and identical every run; a fixed workflow gets the same result with less cost and less unpredictable behavior
Agents are structurally incapable of reliable tool use, so a workflow is the only option that works at all
Only a workflow can use the Claude API's tool-use feature; agents cannot register tools
An agent architecture always requires a manager delegating to a subagent hierarchy, which this simple task doesn't justify

explanation: The correct counterargument is a cost/complexity one: identical, fully-known steps get no benefit from agent flexibility, so the workflow wins on cost and predictability. The other three options invent false technical limitations -- agents can call tools reliably, both workflows and agents use the same tool-use feature, and a single agent never requires a manager/subagent hierarchy. Each sounds like a plausible technical fact but fails on that basis alone.
author: v1-new
